chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked them (peace be upon them) about a man who became ill and did not fast until another month of Ramadan reached him. They said: 'If he had recovered and then delayed before the next fasting reached him, he should fast the one he reached and give charity for each day with a mudd of food for a poor person, and he must make up the missed days. But if he remained ill until another month of Ramadan reached him, he should fast the one he reached and give charity for the first [year] for each day a mudd for a poor person, and there is no making up [the fasts] upon him.'

key_terms.فِدْيَةٌ: charity payment for missed fasts (implied by context of charity for each day)
key_terms.مُدٍّ: a specific measure of volume for food

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for someone who missed Ramadan fasts due to illness and did not make them up before the next Ramadan?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between temporary and chronic illness in Shia jurisprudence, emphasizing that continuous invalidation of the obligation to *qada* (make-up fasting) applies only when the illness persists through the entire subsequent Ramadan. The requirement of *fidya* (feeding a poor person) alongside *qada* for delayed recovery highlights the dual penalty for neglecting the obligatory fast, a nuance often discussed in contrast to the Hanafi view which may limit *fidya* to specific cases. This ruling underscores the Shia principle that the exemption from *qada* is strictly tied to the duration of the impediment relative to the lunar cycle.
